Josephine Klein

Josephine Klein

Josephine Klein  

What did I know about Paula Heimann before I read this collection of her essays? Only her helpful and humane papers on countertransference - though it is still surprising to me that these modest beginnings, illuminating a hitherto badly understood experience, eventually helped move countertransference into the forefront of psychoanalytic thinking.

Knowing so little, I was the more grateful for the two introductory essays. From Pearl King's Introductory Memoir: ‘Paula Heimann's quest for her own identity as a psychoanalyst’, I learnt among other interesting details that she trained in Berlin in the Freudian tradition, came to England and had a second analysis with Melanie Klein (the first was with Theodor Reik), but gradually moved away from Klein into an independent position. From editor Margret Tonnesmann I gained an account of the evolution of her views on early infantile development, on technique and on her differences from Melanie Klein. I found Tonnesmann's summary of Heimann's views on projective identification and related processes particularly valuable (pp. 12-13).

International Review of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 17, Part 3, 1990

If Oedipus Was An Egyptian

Joan Raphael-Leff

Freud's archaeological collection peopled his work rooms with sublimated expressions of eternal, universal desires. I suggest here that these tangible remnants from the long buried past resonated with psychic representations and dream figures in Freud's own internal world, which, nevertheless, were not always consciously available to him. Despite a fascination with Egyptology evidenced in his antiquities, library and less conventional works, Freud focused on aspects of the Greek oedipal legend in his theoretical writing, neglecting Egyptian myths associated with ‘prehistoric’ realms of the archaic mother and Osirian/Mosaic father. I argue that convergence of traumatic events in his early childhood contributed to this delimiting Graeco-Roman filter, and that accessibility to the ‘dark continent’ was hampered by resistances his own self-analysis could not penetrate but which may have been worked through in the transference had he had an analyst other than himself.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 71, Part 3, 1990

A New Look at the Theory of Melanie Klein

Ruth Stein

This paper tries to show that Melanie Klein's theory can very profitably be viewed as a descriptive theory of strong emotions rather than an instinct or developmental theory. Furthermore, since in Klein's thinking feelings ‘create’ objects, the primacy of feelings in this theory is central. The paper contains a short chronological study of Klein's formulations of psychic phenomena in terms of affects. It is also maintained that the paranoid-schizoid and the depressive positions are constellations of affects and of reactions to them; that psychic development is essentially in terms of the capacity to tolerate feelings, and that the basic conflict in mental life is between feelings of love and hate and associated feelings. Such a view solves many of the conceptual difficulties of Kleinian theory and in addition promises rewarding insights into the world of feelings.

Thomas Szasz, Mental Illness and Psychotherapy

Robin Brown

Robin Brown

14 Ambra Vale West, Clifton Wood, Bristol BS8 4RD.

Robin Brown  

Strictly speaking, disease or illness can only affect the body; hence there can be no mental illness.

This is the first of Thomas Szasz' ten points summarising his famous and notorious book The Myth of Mental Illness (Szasz 1961). If it is true, it seems to me to have profound implications for the way we conceptualise the psychotherapeutic process which we practise. I think it is in more than our terminology that we imply a medical model of our work. The words themselves - patient, treatment, cure, neurosis, schizophrenia and so on - convey an implicit agreement with the localisation of psychotherapy in the area of social activity which may be called ‘healing the sick’. But if the patients are not sick, and hence not patients in an ordinary sense, then this perception of our work will not do, and in the interests of consistency we are required to re-evaluate the processes going on in our consulting rooms.

Some months ago I saw a television programme in which Szasz argued his position with the BBC's house psychiatrist Anthony Clare and Ian Kennedy who is a law professor with interests in medical ethics. Clive James was in the chair. At the time it felt to me like watching a tadpole oversee two minnows fighting with a shark. Szasz' name was known to me only peripherally; he was the strange American psychiatrist with outlandish ideas about mental illness. He had never been seriously discussed in my training, and I rarely came across references to his work in the literature. And yet on hearing him speak I was impressed, in fact almost spellbound. His ideas seemed reasonable, well argued; his opponents missed the point and looked weak by comparison. More than this, though, Szasz seemed to be presenting a radical change of perspective on a recurrent problem I have concerning the nature of my work, just what it is I am doing in my sessions as a psychotherapist. Here was the promise of a paradigm shift in psychology which relieved me of the idea I was curing someone of something, an idea which always made me feel somewhat fraudulent. Further, Szasz seemed to offer a profound demystification; the idea of strange illnesses of the psyche is not a necessary or useful one, and we can conceptualise human mental life without it. I wanted to find out more.

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

Three papers on envy were given at the Conference of The Institute of Psychotherapy and Counselling. The number of related emotional states which orbit within the gravitational field of the concept of envy seems to be large; it is a ‘base passion, drawing the worst passions in its train’: rivalry, competitiveness, jealousy, separation anxiety and the constructive aspects of destructiveness. The close connections that exist between these various painful mental states demonstrated by these papers do seem to confirm for envy the central position that it has classically had within psycho-analysis, in the form of penis envy. As one of the forms, perhaps the worst form, of animosity to life, it is important to chart the routes by which emotional movement towards the other related and ultimately assertively creative powers can take place.

Developmental steps were the intricate topic of last year's Public Lecture given by Margot Waddell. The way in which psychological processes of maturation can be reflected in works of art, notably the novel, is one possible way of looking at the validity of psychological ideas. George Eliot provides a rich source of prepsychoanalytic insights, but Margot Waddell mines these works of imagination for their revelation of the contemporary concept of mental growth through containment of the passions.

It is not only words which have meanings. Andrea Sabbadini argues lucidly for the value of silences. They have a meaning, representing the places for words which would have been there had they not been prevented from utterance. Thus silence is more than resistance, but a complex and delicate balance of phantasy, particularly about the psychotherapist - and to be listened to. Interestingly, Esme Towse explores the role of music when words won't do. If the communication between the psycho-analyst's unconscious and his patient's unconscious is what matters, then music (and maybe silences) can function when words fail, or may even be clearer when words obfuscate.

To Hyphen or Not to Hyphen

John Rowan

John Rowan

John Rowan  

Dear Sir

Could I just draw to your attention a small but significant point about the subediting and proofreading of the Journal. The article by J Susan Kelen on the ego and the self has been mangled by a persistent error. One of the great contributions of Heinz Kohut was the introduction of the term ‘selfobject’. This is printed thus to indicate that at the particular stage to which Kohut refers there is not a connection or a link or a tie between self and object - they are confused and identified. This shows up in therapy as a selfobject transference with a number of special aspects, as Kelen informs us. But in the article as printed this technical term is printed (every time!) as ‘self-object’, thus defeating the whole aim of the exercise. It seems that the subeditor had a set of rules about hyphens, and simply altered the manuscript to suit these general rules which are of course totally irrelevant and maiming in this particular case. I do think it is up to you as editor to watch out for this sort of thing and intercept it at an early stage. If you should print this letter, for example, do check on this point rather carefully, as otherwise it will read rather strangely!

Also I'm a bit surprised that you published the article by Liam Clarke making a mock of Rational-Emotive Therapy (RET). It seems a bit cheap and easy to me. Also, in your editorial, you mention the content of this article by referring to - ‘the more ghastly scenes towards which the humanistic approach may appear to point’- while of course RET is not, and has never been counted as, a humanistic approach. It is one of the cognitive approaches, like the cognitive therapy of Aaron Beck and the personal construct therapy of George Kelly.

Cognitive-Analytic Therapy: Active Participation in Change (A New Integration in Brief Psychotherapy) by Anthony Ryle (with contributions from Amanda Poynton and Bee Brockman). Published by John Wiley and Sons Ltd, 1990; 267 pages; £25.00 hardback.

Kristina Stanton

Kristina Stanton

Kristina Stanton  

Anthony Ryle, consultant psychotherapist at St Thomas's Hospital, London, has been developing a innovative therapy called Cognitive-Analytic Therapy (CAT) over the last twelve years, and this book provides a comprehensive introduction to the theory and method that has evolved. This is an important development in applied psychoanalysis in the tradition of time-limited work begun by Ferenczi and Balint (Balint 1972) and will be essential reading for mental health professionals involved in brief psychotherapy.

CAT follows a format of sixteen sessions, the first four of which are aimed at reformulating the patients' problems in terms of ‘procedures’. ‘Procedures’ are the mechanisms by which patients perpetuate neurotic difficulties, thought disorders, dissatisfying relationships and symptoms. There are three sorts of procedures, traps, snags and dilemmas, which Ryle elaborates with detailed clinical examples. Patients are requested to keep a diary during therapy and rate their own progress. With the help of the therapist, they discover how such procedures operated during their past, how they influence their present relationships, and how they are at work in the transference. Such discovery ‘gives back the meaning of past experiences by validating previously disallowed sadness or anger and recruits them [the patients] to active work’ (p. 221). Through this, they gain a ‘powerful sense of personal efficacy’ (p. 220). The remaining sessions are then spent recognising a few specific procedures, called target problem procedures (TPP's), and exploring alternative ways of feeling, thinking and behaving.

It has frequently been noted that many professionals providing therapy in the public sector often mix psychoanalytic, behavioural and cognitive models, usually under the pressure of time and expense (Douglas 1989). Until now the view of Balint and other psychoanalytic innovators has been accepted, namely that there is no adequate metatheory to explain what is special about brief psychotherapy. Anthony Ryle, however, has directly answered this dilemma by reformulating object relations theory through relating it to new developments in cognitive information processing theories. These new developments include explaining how affect and cognition are intimately connected, and seek to understand the interplay of unconscious elements in the complex fabric of mental life. It may surprise some psychoanalysts to know, for example, that cognitive theorists now fully appreciate how the intrapsychic is essentially formed by interpersonal experience.

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

The & physical life of the foetus, or the physical life of a culture, the attempts to make psycho-analytic and psychotherapeutic ideas relevant outside the consulting room have been continuous throughout the practice of psychotherapy. Robert Whyte has attempted to follow the conversion of the physiological interactions between the mother's womb and the foetus into the psychological interaction of the infant with the mother. The physiological proto-object becomes the infant's psychological object at a point coinciding with the severance of the umbilical cord. There is a large body of interest in this cosmic moment of the psychological birth of the new human being, though some would assert that it is not a matter for psychological discovery but more one for spiritual contemplation. It leaves us with the question of what are the possibilities of knowledge of these remote but extraordinarily personally intimate occurrences. We do not yet have the psychological equivalent of the radio telescope which was a profound quantum leap in the investigation of outer space. Helga Coulter in her prize essay raises questions of epistemology about the infant - how can we know about it? or what makes us convinced that our knowledge is true? She is concerned about the nature of the knowledge that comes out of observation which is knowingly an influence upon what is observed.

We could get along with a general shrug of the shoulders and a resignation to having a good-enough though not perfect method of understanding in the sensitive area of investigating responding human subjects. However psychotherapists (of most kinds, I think, and especially psycho-analytic ones) tend to think the participant observer role is of a special kind, and that the knowledge that comes from it is itself of a special kind, perhaps different epistemologically from ‘objective’ knowledge.

At the same time, we observe our culture in the same participating way. It is natural for psychotherapists to think cultural, political and social happenings in their own terms, those of the unconscious, transference etc. Is this just a kind of ‘ethnocentric’ reaction of the psychotherapy culture? We would tend to disagree and argue that something that can be validly said about individuals must have relevance to the events that occur within a collection of individuals; but the difficulties are considerable. Rob Weatherill asks some questions: what is the relationship between cultural and social activity and the intra-psychic internal world of the participating individuals?

The Psychotherapy Register

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny  

UKSCP was inaugurated in January 1989 as a sequel to the ‘Rugby’ Psychotherapy Conference, itself a sequel to the Sieghart Committee. In 1990 UKSCP resolved to establish psychotherapy as a separate profession and to seek to establish itself as the competent authority in relation to E.C. regulations, present and impending, which regulate the freedom of movement of professional people in the E.C. The key to being a competent authority lies mainly in holding a register for the profession.

With increasing interest in the sequence and process of moving towards the formation of a psychotherapy register, I thought it might be helpful to spell out the process that will be taking place over the next few months.

Draft proposals for entry requirements and curriculum content were circulated earlier this year to all our Member Organisations for critical comment. At a Special General Meeting, held on 12 October 1991, we reached agreement on two critical issues. The first, that psychotherapy should be a post-graduate profession so that we fit into the first draft directive of the E.C. which concerns what are called ‘liberal and social professions’. The second, that psychotherapy training requires analysis and self-exploration for the benefit of the client as well as the practitioner. This means that people who wish to train in psychotherapy must have a qualification which is of degree level, although it need not necessarily be academic, and that they must undertake a personal analytical or self-examination procedure, appropriate to the kind of psychotherapy that they will be training for. We have not yet agreed on the outlines of the curriculum contents that will be required for trainings, but there is broad agreement in the written responses to our original proposals, so that it will not be difficult to formulate acceptable standards for curriculum content.

We are now in a position to decide upon the functions and therefore, the structure of the Registration Committee and we will be putting proposals to the Annual General Meeting in January 1992. We will have to do an appraisal of costs and draw up a realistic budget which will form the basis of applications for grants from appropriate Government departments. We hope to have a good chance of getting a grant for what will, in effect, be a national project of forming a register of psychotherapists. We should, therefore, be in a position to appoint or elect the new Registration Committee at the Annual General Meeting of January 1993. The new Registration Committee will then set up and maintain a register of the practising members of the Member Organisations of UKSCP. This register will not have any official status but we hope that it will achieve official recognition in due course.

The European Federation of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy (EFPP)

Brian Martindale

Brian Martindale

Room 123, Tavistock Centre, 120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Brian Martindale  

A Brief History

The EFPP is essentially a British initiative concerned with public sector psychoanalytic psychotherapy that seems to have touched upon a recognised need in our European neighbours and colleagues. Its origins are inextricably linked with the development of the Association for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy in the British Health Service (APP).

The APP

The APP was founded in 1981 by a group of psychoanalysts working as Consultant Psychotherapists in the NHS. It rapidly became a multidisciplinary organisation with full members having completed training in specified training organisations and employed at senior levels within the public services. The main concerns of the APP stem from the limited amount of skilled psychoanalytic psychotherapy available in the public services in Britain, except in a few centres of excellence. Furthermore there has been a relative failure of the established professions of psychiatry and psychology to address seriously these issues in training and service provision. From early days the APP has also had in mind those members of the traditional caring professions who find the ideas and understandings of psychoanalysis (and techniques derived from it) invaluable in their daily work. The APP has encouraged and supported such persons through associate membership. The need for the APP is illustrated by its rapid growth such that after ten years there are 425 associate and full members.

As well as developing a journal Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy the APP has been organising important conferences in different parts of the country on themes relevant to work in the NHS. Appropriately for the aims of the APP, some of these themes have been related to the politics of the provision of public sector psychoanalytic psychotherapy. One example of this was a conference in November 1989 debating the issues for and against the development of a separate non-medical adult psychotherapy discipline in the NHS along the lines of the, now well-established and reputable, child psychotherapy discipline. The council of the APP has played an important part in trying to promote this development as it sees this as a necessary step if the NHS is to begin to face the severe shortage of trained therapists for the large numbers of patients who could gain benefit for themselves and their families and society if treated.

Psychoanalysis and Dogmatism

David Smith

David Smith

David Smith  

As its title implies, Patrick Casement's Further Learning From the Patient (1990)* is the sequel to his earlier On Learning From the Patient (1985). Like its predecessor, Further Learning deals mainly with issues surrounding analytic technique. Further Learning is a slim volume which is clearly and engagingly written. Like On Learning From the Patient, Further Learning represents the progressive edge of the standard Freudian-Kleinian-Object Relational paradigm. It will be of interest to those already committed to mainstream psychoanalysis and will be accessible to those who are looking for an accessible introduction to liberal mainstream analytic technique and who have some background knowledge of psychoanalytic theory.

The central preoccupation of Further Learning is the issue of psychoanalytic dogmatism. Throughout the book, Casement expresses concern about the prevalence of dogmatic thinking in psychoanalysis and strives to develop a non-dogmatic approach to theory and technique. I do not think that Casement's concern is misplaced for the question of psychoanalytic dogmatism is, in essence, the question of whether or not we have rational grounds for believing psychoanalytic propositions about the human mind. This, in turn, has profound implications for clinical psycho-analysis. If our belief in psychoanalytic theory is primarily dogmatic rather than rational, what right have we to treat patients using a method derived from this theory? Why should patients entrust themselves to our care?

Laudable as Casement's anti-dogmatic stance is, I will argue that it does not provide an adequate answer to the problem of psychoanalytic dogmatism. It is only by pushing the analysis further that we can determine the true locus of dogmatism within psychoanalysis and devise strategies to eliminate - or at least minimise - it. However, as I will show, the remedy required must call into question the validity of a large number of widely accepted psychoanalytic doctrines and undercuts the psychoanalytic pluralism which Casement recommends as an antidote for psychoanalytic dogmatism.

Hobson's Choice: Personal Analysis and Supervision in the Training of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapists

Thomas Freeman

Thomas Freeman

75 Ballybentragh Road, Muckamore, Antrim BT41 2HS.

Thomas Freeman  

Personal analysis on a five times weekly basis continued for at least three years and regular (weekly) supervision constitute the core of a training in psychoanalytic psychotherapy. For many years supervision of therapeutic work has been undertaken by a trained and experienced practitioner other than the psychoanalyst conducting the trainee's personal analysis. This happens at the Tavistock Clinic, at the Scottish Association of Psychoanalytical Psychotherapists and the British Association of Psychotherapists. It is a practice which is difficult to follow in those parts of the United Kingdom where there are few trained psychoanalysts and analytic psychotherapists. What is to be done in an area where there is only one accredited psychoanalyst? Does this mean that suitably qualified candidates are to be deprived of a training in psychoanalytic psychotherapy? There is precedence, however, for the simultaneous analysis and supervision of a trainee by the one psychoanalytic practitioner.

The requirement that the analyst conducting a personal (training) analysis should not be the analysand's supervisor followed from a recommendation made originally by the Psychoanalytic Institutes in Berlin and Vienna. This was long ago and the fact that it was a source of controversy has been forgotten. Ferenczi and his Hungarian colleagues, of whom Balint was one, doubted the wisdom of this separation of functions. In their opinion a candidate's counter-reactions (Glover 1955) and his countertransferences (Reich 1951) were more readily accessible to analysis when the one analyst conducted both the personal analysis and the supervision. The difference of opinion on this subject was never officially resolved. The London Institute of Psychoanalysis decided in 1947 that different analysts must undertake the candidate's personal analysis and supervision of his clinical work. Balint (1948) believed that this arbitrary decision was not based on a thorough study of the issue. Despite this ruling, the Training Committee of the London Institute allowed Balint, after 1947, to supervise his analysand's first training case. He continued to do so until he died. This practice was also permitted by the Topeka and Washington Psychoanalytic Institutes during the early years of their existence. There are therefore sound precedents for the practice of combining the functions of analyst and supervisor.

[[RunningHead]]

When is a Pervert Not a Pervert?

Rachel Cunningham

Rachel Cunningham

Rachel Cunningham  

My purpose here is to argue for an open-minded but rigorous way of thinking about homosexuality psychodynamically and to investigate the real and imagined problems it brings up in relation to suitability for psychoanalytic training. I propose that to exclude a person from such training because of his or her homosexuality per se indicates the presence of phobia in certain areas of the analytic establishment, namely in the Freudian-Kleinian stream of the BAP and in the Institute of Psycho-Analysis. As far as I know, only these two institutes have an official line on this issue though other training establishments also seem to be affected by prejudice, making it difficult for a homosexual to brave the choppy waters' of training without compromise and discomfort.

Although my experience of a psychoanalytic environment is confined to London, it seems that the psychoanalytic view of homosexuality which I am criticising is widespread, judging from the literature published here and abroad. There are exceptions. The Lacanian school, for instance, sees human sexuality as constructed within cultural, linguistic frameworks rather than being a biological ‘given’ vulnerable to distortion from its natural, heterosexual state. I am also aware, from discussions with individual analysts and psychotherapists, that there is a new trend of thought focusing on perversions more as an issue of character structure and sado-masochistic dynamics than as a problem of object choice. That is, perversion is seen as cutting across both homosexuality and heterosexuality. The focus is on the presence or absence in the personality of, for instance, narcissism, depressive concern, the tendency to part or whole object relating, to anaclitic, dependent relating, and so on. These are all characteristics and qualities which can be found in homosexuals and heterosexuals and in their modes of relating to others. This way of viewing sexualities does not attempt to blur the distinctions between them but to tabulate more clearly what health and perversity consist in. And it becomes clear that the choice of sexual object does not necessarily denote the type of personality of the chooser. That is, one cannot infer from the fact that a person's choice is homosexual that s/he has a perverse character organisation. Perversion is seen as a mixture of addiction and choice, a tending to destructiveness and the bad which is accompanied by awareness … ‘Evil be thou my good’.

Hating the patient is seen as a natural part of any psychotherapeutic practice. Its emergence may be related to work with difficult or demanding patients. Journal of Analytical Psychology, Volume 36, Number 2, 1991

The Oedipal Complex in Adolescence

Hugh Gee

In this paper I have re-examined the story of Oedipus in order to look at the possible parallels with the adolescent who is struggling towards maturity. Drawing from a number of differing sources, I started by retelling the story itself. I then highlighted a number of themes which seem important in the psychology of adolescence; particularly their movement towards consciousness. The first of these themes was ‘abandonment’. Under this heading I tried to show how a ‘sense of abandonment’ may be one of the dynamics that activates the hero archetype, which was the next theme that I examined in both its positive and negative aspects. In line with Jung's approach, I then discussed what seems to me to be the ‘purpose’ of the hero, namely, that it facilitates the developing awareness of inner strengths which, in turn, helps the adolescent in his need to separate from the family. Later in the paper I discuss the resolution of the Oedipus Complex in relation to the adolescent's incestuous wishes, and show how important Jung's concept of ‘sacrifice’ is in emphasising the positive side of growth. I ended the paper by discussing the possible role that myths may play in the transference/countertransference relationship.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 72, Part 1, 1991

Body Image, Sexuality and the Psychotic Core

Egle Laufer

The mental representation of the body - that is, the body image - is a basic element of the person's relationship to himself as well as to reality. From a developmental point of view the body image only becomes finally integrated to form the basis of the person's sexual and gender identity at the end of adolescence. This final body image can contain distortions compared to the person's real body (as viewed by others) and thus can represent a break with some aspects of external reality.

In this paper I use material from the analyses of two patients, one adult and one adolescent, to show the compelling quality of the need to maintain a specific body image, and how it becomes related to their sexuality. I also discuss how, when the body image is one that is distorted, it forms a psychotic core to the personality in that it must affect the person's relationship to external reality.

Comment on Robert Whyte's Paper ‘Giving and Taking’

John Rowan

John Rowan

John Rowan  

I have been reading the paper entitled ‘Giving and Taking: The foetal-maternal placental junction as a prototype and precursor of object relations’ in the Spring 1991 issue of the Journal. The case vignette is perfectly acceptable and interesting but I want to take issue with some of the argument leading up to it.

The author says: ‘Although Stern (1985) has shown that perceptual memories of sounds heard in the womb exist in young babies, the idea of any mental functioning complex enough to be called psychological life occurring before birth seems very doubtful to me’. To start with, Stern is not a researcher into prenatal life (he has done some research on mother-baby interactions) and to quote him as if he were is misleading. In any case he says hardly anything about the matter. The author does not mention the people who do write about this, such as Verny (1982) and Ridgway (1989).

He says ‘Laing (1983) joins with Freud in considering that Rank's theory of birth trauma has no place in the scientific scheme of things’. This seems an odd misreading: the truth is that in that book Laing embraces not only the theory of birth trauma (see also Janov 1983, Grof 1985), but also the theory of foetal trauma, implantation trauma and conception trauma, and quotes people like Mott (1959), Peerbolte (1975), Swartley (1978) and Lake (1980) in support of such ideas. He also quotes Winnicott as being in favour of the idea of birth trauma (p. 94). Perhaps the author of this article is not familiar with the work of Laing, because he says many of the same things in his earlier book The Facts of Life.

None of the medical textbooks known to me mention a distinction between a foetal placenta and a maternal placenta. It seems that different authorities have somewhat different views as to the precise nomenclature here. The whole of the placenta, as I understand it, is foetal material, and comes from the original fertilised gamete. It all belongs to the foetus, in that sense, and merely pushes out villi into the uterine wall, which responds by forming sinuses for the easy transfer of maternal blood. The mother, as it were, responds to the placenta but does not have a placenta. As I say, it may be that some specialists divide up the matter differently but I think this is the prevalent view.

The Plural Psyche by Andrew Samuels. Published by Routledge, 1989; 253 pages; E12. 95.

Val Richards

Val Richards

Val Richards  

In his earlier book Jung and the Post Jungians (1985), Andrew Samuels focused on the similarities between the many and the one - how most contemporary trends in psychoanalysis and psychotherapy were prefigured in the ideas and practice of C G Jung. Now The Plural Psyche is a celebration of the many and the different where Samuels applies what he calls the ‘tool’ of pluralism to a range of concerns in depth psychology, extending from the microcosm of the intra-psychic world to the interpersonal world of the family and beyond. His study takes in such issues as sexuality, gender identity, borderline disorder, private and public morality, concentrating especially on the figures of the father and the analyst.

A pluralistic attitude is one which positively upholds and maintains the contradictions and differences within a subject or field, in the belief that ‘truth’ is multi-faceted and not reducible to a single position. Samuels writes (p. ix):

Pluralism is an approach to conflict that tries to reconcile differences without imposing a false synthesis on them and, above all, without losing sight of the particular value and truth of each element in the conflict.

Implicit in this approach are both the structuralist idea that a subject is defined by the oppositions between its interrelated parts and, further, the post-structuralist claim (supported by Samuels) that meaning is multi-faceted and over-determined and, above all, governed by the subjectivity of the enquirers.

Pluralism, as an instrument, seems also to connect directly with three key Jungian concepts:

his vision of the psyche as the relationship between conscious and unconscious, constituted by the collision of opposites (Humbert 1988, p. 117):

Wholeness doesn't mean having or being everything; it means, rather, living in a structure within which opposites are at play.

the centrality of metaphor - that all theory, and indeed all language, is metaphorical and that the metaphorical may be a more valid witness than the literal, to the spirit and complexity of a subject. Samuels, as will be seen, is especially concerned with the interdependence of the literal and metaphorical. (3) the function and nature of archetypes as both culturally and historically determined.

Josephine Lomax-Simpson

Josephine Lomax-Simpson

Josephine Lomax-Simpson  

I am confident that this description of the personality of the author and his struggle with his chronic illness deserves to be read by patients who suffer from similar illnesses and by those who care for them.

Cecil Todes who is both a psychiatrist and psycho-analyst states that Parkinson's disease is ‘a chronic degenerative disorder affecting at least one in a thousand of the population before the age of forty’. As it is considered to be a relatively common disease I have little doubt that a second edition of this book will be forthcoming. In such circumstances perhaps the following suggestions could be considered.

The effect and function of drugs are of primary clinical importance and I read with interest the role of what Todes describes as the four ‘f s - fight, flight, food and sexual behaviour. In this area it would have been helpful to have known more about the fourth ‘f and ways of coming to terms with the sexual limitations in the lives of those suffering from chronic neurological disease.

Likewise, although he has come to terms with not wishing to be the ‘guinea pig’ for every possible new cure, he does not seem to have considered signing a ‘Living Will’ (the Voluntary Euthanasia Society's Advance Declaration as a protection against unwanted ‘medicated survival’). I am left wondering why not? Certainly the moment of cardiac arrest was one where the need to ‘officiously strive to keep alive’ was debatable. In similar circumstances I would not have wished to have been kept alive. Donald Winnicott always prayed that he ‘was alive when he died’ and my prayer has always been: ‘Please God let me only have to die once’. I wonder what is Cecil Todes' prayer?

Perhaps the neurologists are right and that Pergolide may cause arrhythmia. Having taken it with benefit for so long, surely it was worth continuing with the risk rather than deprive himself of the pleasure of the ‘on’ as opposed to so much ‘off’.

The account ends on a positive note with a ‘Fresh Start’. The description of the use of music - in the hospital rehabilitation programme, at the holistic centre at St Marylebone Church and ultimately in rhythm creating a ‘dialogue in sound’ with a music therapist from Germany is a living testimony in itself.

Adrian Williams

Adrian Williams

Adrian Williams  

Freud's ‘Oedipus complex’ indicates the importance of myths in the development of psychoanalytic theories; indeed Bion reserves a whole line of his grid for dream thoughts, dreams and myths (row C). The Biblical Genesis is so rich in myths of our culture that it is surprising more has not been made of it (as far as I am aware) by psychoanalysts and those using psychoanalytic insights which have diffused into other fields. Freud might have made use of any of these myths - Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, Noah, David and Goliath - as a starting point for exploring the inner world. He chose the Greek myths possibly because his upbringing allowed him to view these more objectively.

Eric Rhode's book is firmly founded in Genesis, which he uses for an internal dialogue with what Bion would call the ‘ineffable’. He writes: ‘We all find a common Adamic inheritance … My Adam lives in the realms of intuition and magic’. Rhode says his book is a type of ‘anti-biography’ - a term which he uses to describe his observation of an interaction between his own deeply primitive inner self and the Genesis myth of creation, a sort of pre-symbolic consciousness. Genesis conveys the bright sun and dark shade of what he calls ‘psychotic literalism’ or, in Bionic terms, pre-natal realism. As Rhode points out, literary tradition is steeped in the Genesis myths as in Milton's Paradise Lost; but he says here these are worked on from a ‘neurotic’ rather than a ‘psychotic’ primitive angle.

From War Babies to Grandmothers - Forty-Eight Years in Psychoanalysis by Ilse Hellman. Published by Karnac Books and the Institute of Psycho-Analysis, London, 1990; 254 pages; £16.00 paperback.

Josephine Lomax-Simpson

Josephine Lomax-Simpson

Josephine Lomax-Simpson  

This is a book I recommended to people during my recent visit to Melbourne, Sydney, Perth and Singapore. I feel it should be available in the non-professional libraries as it demonstrates the author's ‘continuity of concern’. The effect of this policy in her work has paid undoubted dividends in the lives of the children she treated. Perhaps the same could be said for her psychoanalytic colleagues. The value of intense study over a protracted period of time is often neglected today and regarded as a luxury rather than a sound investment for the future.

I also believe that the personality of the psychoanalyst is important. This book reflects Miss Hellman's personality - a sprightly individual of 80 years surrounded by young people and sharing not only wisdom and expertise but also a very real sense of humour and reality. Contributions are made by colleagues including Liselotte Frankl. Sadly she has died but is remembered with affection by those child patients with whom she worked with skill and care.

This collection of papers provides a valuable insight into the work of the Hampstead War Nurseries, the Anna Freud Centre and the Adolescent Study Group at the Hampstead Child Therapy Clinic. The discerning reader will also be aware of the role of psychoanalysis in an important stage of development.

[[RunningHead]]

Commentary by a Psychoanalytical Family Therapist

Jorge Thomas

Jorge Thomas

Jorge Thomas  

I have been asked to comment on a family therapy session where the use of ‘ritual’ as

95

a therapeutic process to mark and facilitate an important transition in the lives of members of a family is discussed.

The material that I saw is a very moving account of what feels a real experience of loss, separation and mourning, helped by a gentle and firm therapist who enabled the family to move from pathological mourning to real sadness. The therapist used what for me are ‘interpretations in action and movement’ which is a different perspective from the one I would like to follow. My comments on the family evolution and the session described offer a different point of view, not better or worse, than the theoretical model used by the therapist. I think that the symptomatic presentation could be seen as the experience of the family's shared, unconscious fantasies or defence mechanisms, and the way they have been used by the family members to modify or evade the reality of their experience of loss and pain.

The first question one has to ask oneself is, who is the family who is consulting, is it the family of origin, which is probably no longer the real family, or the parents and their partners, and their children? It is a difficult decision. I tend to choose to see those who are living together because I think that those persons are the ones who will probably go on enacting, in a shared manner, some of their unconscious fantasies about their anxiety and their defence mechanisms.

The family could be described also as a group oscillating between a mental state of a basic assumption and a work group:

Basic Assumption Fight and Flight: The parents end their relationship, start new relationships, and very soon there is an acrimonious atmosphere between them that was not resolved until the time of their consultation.
Basic Assumption Pairing: There are clearly new sexual pairs formed, which might be seen as an attempt by the family to deal with intense anxieties in the parental couple and with those of Jane at a time when her oedipal anxieties must have been intense, with consequences not only for her but in the stability of the parental couple and their oedipal resolutions.
Basic Assumption Dependency: my impression is that the parents depend on Jane to keep them together; she has chosen unconsciously to have symptoms in the area of eating, a behaviour which is safer and might bring them all together whereas other areas, like sexual behaviour, have separated and ended her family unit.

In my assessment I would like to know how mental functions are distributed in the internal space of each member of the family and in the group space as a whole. Together with that I would want to know the anatomy of the shared experience of anxiety, what distribution it has, where it originated and how it affects all the members of the family. It seems from the description given that the family has been operating under a very intense persecutory anxiety for some time. The mental functions I refer to are of two main groups, integrative and projective functions (Meltzer, Harris)

[[RunningHead]]

Psycho-Analysis and Psycho-Analytic Psychotherapy Training in Northern Ireland

Richard Wieland

Richard Wieland

Richard Wieland  

I am reminded of an unforgettable moment in my London-based therapy, some ten years ago, when I announced I was considering taking up a lecturing post in Northern Ireland. My Jungian analyst seemed to jump out of her chair as she retorted: ‘You must be mad!’ It was a moment I have never forgotten although its meanings seem to multiply as the years go by.

A necessary if not sufficient condition for developing a psycho-analytic movement is, I suppose, a single psycho-analyst. That is what we have in Northern Ireland, a ratio of some 1:11/Z million. And we have been well served with Dr Tom Freeman who settled here - if that is the right word - in 1968 (Freeman 1988).

‘Let a man build a better mouse-trap than his neighbour and the world shall beat a broad path to his door, though he live in the heart of a deep wood’, my father used to say to me as a young boy, echoing his own father's words and those of Emerson.

I hope this is a not inappropriate metaphor to convey something of the position of those half-dozen or so of us, who slowly but surely have found their way to Dr Freeman's door since the early 1980's, determined to do what we could and can to make connections with the world of psycho-analysis, and to establish something of a psycho-analytic movement in Northern Ireland, our location and circumstances notwithstanding.

In short, we wish to connect but how? How are we doing it? What are the difficulties? What are the excitements?

It should be evident that our present problems are first and foremost ones of trainings and practical possibilities. Whilst it has been possible for a group of us to undergo a personal classical analysis, the opportunity of weekly supervision of two training cases in classical analysis by two different training analysts has not been possible to date. Our one analyst has both analysed us and supervised our first cases.

There are, of course, precedents for this system of training. As Dr Freeman puts it, with a glint in his eyes: ‘We follow the “Hungarian system” here’. Pedder (1986)

RET - Throwing the Baby out with the Bathwater?

Norman mohan and Ann Macaskill

Ann Macaskill

Ann Macaskill  

We believe RET therapists should take quite seriously the criticisms levelled at RET in Clarke's ‘Personal View’ in the British Journal of Psychotherapy, 7(1), pp. 86-93. We speak as therapists who utilise and value RET in our day-to-day psychotherapeutic practice yet find ourselves distinctly uncomfortable with, and dissatisfied with, some potentially insensitive, aggressive and belittling aspects of RET.

Observation of RET ‘experts’ in action, feedback from teaching seminars and comments from patients, all suggest that, like other brief active directive and focal therapies, great care and sensitivity need to be exercised when utilising RET as otherwise therapists run a high risk of traumatising patients, damaging the therapeutic relationship and forcing patients from therapy.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

AIDS is topical and deathly. Its silence and final, sudden calamity give it a special psychological power. We present three papers concerned with the impact of AIDS on the personality of the sufferer and the carrier of the virus. Lorna Bradley describes her counselling work with those presenting for HIV testing. The worry about the possibility of being HIV positive is itself already a condition amenable to psychological intervention, and counselling at that point creates the possibilities for long-term intervention where necessary. The way the impact of the disease affects the personality is varied. One of the reactions to being HIV positive is a bitter withdrawal, and vengeance against the social shame and condemnation of the sufferer and his sexuality. This phenomenon of revenge is examined in the paper by Hari Maharajh and Patricia Sarkar-Crooks, who argue therefore for the early intervention of the psychiatrist/ psychotherapist in the work with those presenting for testing. The impact of a virtual death sentence as it seems to the patient is compounded by the social reaction they are confronted with. Close relatives and friends in particular, and society in general, combine in moral condemnation of the already traumatised patient by socially shaming and rejecting him. Bernard Ratigan examines the possibilities for providing a helping environment that can go towards mitigating the social trauma to those already facing death.

The social shame attached to sexual deviance has massive detrimental consequences in all sorts of areas of life. Typically, in our own world of psychotherapy, it is often assumed that a ‘deviance’ as definite as homosexuality marks out a personality defect that is severe enough to preclude joining the profession. Homosexuality may be unfairly ‘visible’ as a marker of unsuitability for training; comparable features of deviance in many perverse forms of heterosexuality are often much more hidden, though no less acted-out. ‘Rachel Cunningham's’ long essay debates the difficulties in assessing how much perversion is too much perversion for a trainee in psychotherapy.

The Psychotherapy Register

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny  

There is an increasing interest in the sequence and process of the formation of the psychotherapy register. I thought it might be helpful to spell out the process that will be taking place over the next few months.

The first draft proposals for entry requirements and curriculum contents for trainings have been circulated to all our member organisations for critical comment. We are waiting to hear from them and hope to be able to make some comment in the mid-year mailing which will appear in September.

The major discussion of these criteria will take place at a Special General Meeting called for 12 October when we hope to reach broad agreement on the requirements for entry and training. Additional refinements will appear in a set of regulations to be agreed at the Annual General Meeting in January 1992.

After this, we will be able to decide upon the functions and, therefore, the structure of the Registration Committee. We will have to do an appraisal of costs and draw up a realistic budget which will form the basis of applications for grants from appropriate Government departments. We should stand a good chance of getting a grant for what will, in effect, be a national project of forming a register of psychotherapists.

We should, therefore, be in a position to appoint or elect the new Registration Committee at the Annual General Meeting in January 1993. The new Registration Committee will then set up and maintain a register of the practising members of the Member Organisations of UKSCP. This register will not have any official status but we hope that it will achieve official recognition in due course.

There will have to be a transitional period during which practising psychotherapists can get on to the register by appropriate means to be agreed upon. After an initial transitional period, only those who have completed an approved training will be eligible to be registered. We expect that there will be some form of on-going professional development required in order for psychotherapists to stay on the register. It is quite clear that there will be organisations in membership of UKSCP whose members will not be eligible to be registered as psychotherapists.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 72, Part 2, 1991

Transference Regression and Psychoanalytic Technique with Infantile Personalities

Otto Kernberg

This paper describes a particular form of ‘silent’ regression during the psychoanalytic treatment of infantile personalities (a type of character pathology related to the hysterical personality). This regression is characterized by the development of rapid interchange in the roles enacted in the transference and projected on to the analyst, an apparent ‘disconnexion’ of the transference material from that dominant when the patient is in non-regressed states, and the intensification of the analyst's countertransference reactions. The diagnosis and management of these regressive transferences require a particular interpretive style and strategy outlined in this paper and illustrated with two case vignettes.



International Review of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 18, Part 2, 1991

The Psychoanalytic Semiosis of Absence or the Semiotic Murder of the Mother

Jane van Buren

The image of the semiotic murder of the mother is a metaphor for the odyssey of the human infant as s/he moves from tactile at-onement with mother and the ‘language’ of normal auto-sensuality, and enters into the signifying and symbolic universe of discourse. Freud's emphasis on the father-son relationship as the key experience around which oedipal development takes place, and Lacan's dichotomization of the capacity to use symbols and language from maternal capacities, have seriously deleted women and mother from the central stage of psychoanalytic theory. Melanie Klein's notions of the pre-oedipal played an important part in re-integrating maternal capacities into psychoanalytic theory. Post-Lacanians, Julia Kristeva and Luce Irigaray, have also resuscitated maternal capacities, proposing that the discourse of mother and child has been exiled from the symbolic order. The notion of the ‘black hole’ as a psychic structure of emptiness and meaninglessness is a major factor in understanding the repression of the maternal body and the infant's experience with her.

Brief Psychotherapy with Patients with Refractory Irritable Bowel Syndrome

Elspeth Guthrie

Elspeth Guthrie

Elspeth Guthrie  

The irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common condition consisting of abdominal pain, abdominal distension and an altered bowel habit in the absence of underlying organic pathology. Most people can be helped by conventional medical treatment but a small proportion (15%) run a chronic course with disabling symptoms that are unresponsive to medical intervention. This paper briefly describes a recent randomised, controlled trial of brief psychotherapy in 102 patients with refractory irritable bowel syndrome. The trial showed that two-thirds of people with chronic symptoms of IBS show significant improvement following brief therapy. Six cases of patients seen during the trial are presented to illustrate the nature of the therapy employed and the range of people who can be helped by such an approach. The advantages and inevitable limitations of brief dynamic therapy with IBS patients are then discussed.

The Mother-Observer Relationship: An Examination of the Participant Role of the Observer in Mother-Infant Observation

Helga Coulter

Helga Coulter

167 Sumatra Road, West Hampstead. London NW6 IPN.

Helga Coulter  

The relationship between mother and observer in mother-infant observation as described by Esther Bick is examined. Specifically, the question as to whether this relationship influences what is being observed is considered.

The author gives an account of her own relationship as an observer with a mother. The mother was an epileptic and fell with her baby (then six weeks old) causing the baby to suffer a broken skull. Exploration of events during the period of observation leads to the conclusion that the relationship between the mother and the observer was one of transference. Within this transference the observer seemed to be the mother of the one observed. This together with the effects on the observed mother's unconscious conflict with her own mother due to epilepsy is described.

Given transference in the mother-observer relationship doubts are raised as to the tenability of the attitude of distance and non-interference prescribed for the observer. The conclusion is drawn that, in any case, the role of the observer is a participant role, which poses the epistemological problem of the interference of the observer with the observed.

Lorne Bradley  

It is now widely accepted in medical circles that people being tested for Human Immuno Deficiency Virus (HIV) should receive both pre-test and post-test counselling whatever the result and this practice is now becoming more widespread. Patients are usually offered one pre-test and, if HIV positive, two post-test counselling sessions but rarely more.

The patient who receives a positive test result experiences shock even when this result was anticipated. At that moment life changes from the expected normal sequence of life events into the prospect of living with the fear of dying for the next ten years or so. Shock leads into disbelief, denial, confusion, fear and acute anxiety, followed by loss of hope and the feeling of being out of control. An overwhelming experience with Sue, 21 years old, a patient whom I have seen regularly since she present, and expectation of the future, are all profoundly involved in the task of dealing with this situation. Diagnosis of HIV needs to be seen not as a diagnosis of terminal illness but rather as a prediction of a particular kind of life. It is in this context that the relevance of psychotherapy in the treatment of the whole person, psyche and soma, will be discussed.

In order to write about this subject realistically I will draw from my working experience with Sue, now 21-years-old, a patient whom I have seen regularly since she was tested positive for HIV three years ago.

A young heterosexual woman has been chosen deliberately because there is currently a need to highlight this group which is now increasing in number. HIV and AIDS affect women both as individuals and also within their roles as mothers, wives, health care providers, educators and income providers, within society and within the family. Over one third of all people known to be HIV infected are women, although the image of the young gay man still springs to mind when AIDS is mentioned. Attention will be drawn to: (1) the important role which bisexual people who act out sexually play in the spread of HIV, why they behave in the way they sometimes do; (2) the importance of what happens to people from the time that they are tested and found to be HIV positive, to the time that they actually become ill with full-blown AIDS.

The Psychical Realities of Modern Culture

Rob Weatherill

Rob Weatherill

22 Pine Court, off Newtown Park Avenue, Blackrock, Dublin, Eire.

Rob Weatherill  

The question posed here is a simple one: what contribution does the unconscious make to any given cultural manifestation and how does culture impinge on the stability of the inner world? So much cultural discussion even involving psychological and social issues ignores the impact of the dynamically repressed unconscious. Yet unconscious meanings and significations are always present and operative alongside our conscious and rational thoughts and actions. The avoidance of the intimate relationship between culture and the unconscious makes much public discussion seem bland and sometimes totally misleading. A culture dominated by a scientific logical positivist point of view throws up its hands in horror and disbelief in face of human atrocities. And yet the media are filled daily with news of those insanities.

Another question arises: how can the psychoanalytically oriented observer make an adequate interpretation, observation, comment on any cultural trend without it sounding too predictable, stereotyped or reductionist? This is a familiar problem, and one that psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapists come up against every day with their patients: how to make an interpretation in response to the patient's productions that is both empathic and objective, precise but also open-ended, intelligent but not omniscient, and above all how to reach out to and support that relatively healthy aspect of self in an attempt to expose and dislodge psychopathology. One can only begin to be effective in this respect by allowing oneself to become immersed in the patient's psychical reality, by being a container for his/her projections, and consequently by becoming affected and at the same time or shortly afterwards trying to think about the experience, to grasp some fragments and articulate them. It is only from this sort of perspective that comment can be made on cultural phenomena. My book The Denial of the Psyche is written from a practitioner's point of view. It will therefore be of interest to a wide range of people who are concerned about modern culture, the fate and stability of the self in that culture, and to those who are psychologically minded. But the book does not represent - and this cannot be overstressed - an attempt to reduce modern cultural trends to a handful of prepackaged psychoanalytic interpretations. Neither is it intended to be an academic and theoretical psychocultural critique at one remove from lived reality. A Register of Psychotherapists

Cecilia Clementel-Jones

Cecilia Clementel-Jones

Via le Broccoli IB, 40600 Osteria Grande, Bologna, Italia.

Cecilia Clementel-Jones  

[Italian regulations for a mandatory register for psychotherapists on the basis of the law Ossicini.

The law 56/89 known as Ossicini was passed by the Italian Parliament on 18 February 1989. The first version of this law had been presented to Parliament for the first time in 1977.]

This paper aims to improve understanding and exchanging at an European level and to clarify the present and future situation of psychotherapists' registration in Italy.

The task of clarifying this particularly intricate connection of Chinese boxes worries me since, after having all my psychiatric and psychotherapy training in London, I have been practising and teaching psychotherapy in my home town of Bologna for the last two years. The Chinese boxes I am thinking of are: Italy, Italian medicine, Italian psychology in general, clinical, social psychology and psychotherapy in particular. The latter is principally divided into two areas: various psychoanalytic strands (I am including Lacanians and Jungians amongst them) on one side, and systemic family therapy approaches (Palazzoli-Selvini) on the other. Cognitive, behavioural and other therapies including group therapies are underdeveloped outside the main centres of Milano and Rome.

As has happened in the United States psychodynamic thinking and vocabulary have acquired in Italy a wide cultural appeal and permeated everyday thinking and discourse to an extent which I find weird. It is generally seen as the opposition of the social psychiatry reform movement led by the late Basaglia which has lost support in professional and political quarters.

What I observe regrettably confirms the statement of Moscovici: ‘Psychoanalysis has become a sort of key, utilized by everybody to open all keys of individual, social and political existence’ (Moscovici 1976, p. 177, my translation). This may have happened so quickly here because other reference and belief systems (both religious and political) have suddenly collapsed. In the private sector wild psychotherapy (and I mean wild), particularly the Lacanian strand, has been, and is, a tremendous problem with everybody declaring themselves ‘analysts’.

Conference January 1991: Chairman's Address

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny  

One of the features of this Conference is that the personnel never remain static. This year we again have many new delegates in our midst. In an ideal world they would all have been fully briefed but, even if that were true in all cases, it is just not possible to convey the cut and thrust of our meetings, nor is it possible to cover all the points we have considered over the years. So we must be patient when we are asked a question we think was settled long ago, and we must try to be explicit when we outline our next steps. Please do not hesitate to raise queries and do not be put off if you hear a loud groan from those who have been here before. It is part of healthy development to ask again those questions that all the rest of us may think of as yesterday's problem.

After another year of hard work we have arrived at the next critical point in our development. As you can see from the large number of sheets in your Conference papers, we have a lot of material to think about and a number of important decisions to make. Let me say now that apart from the Section criteria, none of our decisions this weekend will be binding for more than one year. Our job, as usual at these conferences, is to point the way forward and to offer our member organisations a set of specific proposals for them to consider.

The various sub-committees of Council have worked throughout the year and have reported back at each Council meeting. The working papers that you have in front of you now are the fruits of these endeavours. Each year the sub-committees retire and are appointed as required at the first meeting of the new Council early in the new year. This way we can allow for the fact that the membership of the Council changes from year to year and it also allows the new Council to start from a position of democratic strength in relation to its sub-committees, thus enabling Council members to keep control of what is done in their name and on your behalf.

This year we must take a series of votes on whether or not to accept the Sections as defined by their flag statements and published criteria. It is important to note that once a Section has been accepted by Conference, it becomes the arbiter of the kind of psychotherapy it represents. The intention when the constitution was written was that each grouping of psychotherapies should be largely self governing within the broad framework of the federal structure of the conference. So that each kind of psychotherapy could retain its autonomy and be the judge of its own standards whilst forming a professional structure with other kinds of psychotherapy. We shall discuss this tomorrow and then vote in the light of our discussions. In addition this is the moment when the two year period of grace for organisations to join a Section comes to an end. Although it is true that organisations not in a Section will lose their membership, they are free to apply to Conference either to join an existing Section or to create a new Section. Of course they will have to justify either course of action in a way that will be acceptable to the majority of member organisations.

Commentary on the Paper by Cecilia Clementel-Jones on the Italian Register

Karl Figlio

Karl Figlio

Karl Figlio  

I was asked by the Council of the United Kingdom Standing Conference for Psychotherapy (UKSCP) if I would comment on the paper by Clementel-Jones. Although I will consider this paper with UKSCP in mind, my comments are personal and have not been discussed by Council.

For a psychotherapist, the most striking feature of Clementel-Jones's paper is that it is historical. One can see the specific context within which the proposed regulation of psychotherapy has been formed. In Italy mental health services must be understood against the background of the socialist psychiatric reforms - Psichiatria Democratica - initiated in the 1960s by a group of psychiatrists, sociologists and social workers allied with the psychiatrist, Franco Bassaglia; and coming to legislative fruition in 1978 (Jones 1988, Ramon 1985). The law set out to reduce drastically mental hospital inpatients, to switch to community-based services, to emphasise social factors in mental ill-health and rehabilitation, and to minimise stigmatisation and isolation of the emotionally disturbed.

The structural changes brought with them a cooperative approach to mental health work amongst the different professional groups and, with it, the blurring of traditional professional roles and boundaries of authority. The libertarian spirit infused the reforms with a desire to avoid formal professionalism and the individualising of a client's distress, which it aimed to handle as a social problem. This trend led to an ambivalent attitude towards psychotherapy, a reluctance to differentiate various forms of psychotherapy from common sense approaches and a neglect of formal training (Ramon 1985, pp. 198-9).

Clementel-Jones also points out a feature of the education sector which is similar in spirit to these reforms: the requirement that all applicants for a university course, who have a high school diploma, must be accepted. The effect, she argues, has been to push a large number of psychologists, unable to get jobs and untrained in psychotherapy, into the private psychotherapy market.

International Review of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 17, Part 4, 1990

Marion Milner's ‘Answering Activity’ and the Question of Psychoanalytic Creativity

Michael Parsons

This paper was written in honour of Marion Milner's 90th birthday. It traces the development, in her three autobiographical books, A Life of One's Own, An Experiment in Leisure and Eternity's Sunrise, of the idea of an ‘Answering Activity’: the experience of an inner being, both part of oneself and greater than oneself, with which one can make contact through a particular kind of meditative awareness. I also explore the tension between technique and creativity in psychoanalysis and show how they must be kept in equilibrium without sacrificing either one. Milner's account of the ‘Answering Activity’ can help us towards the theory of psychoanalytic creativity which this requires.



International Review of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 17, Part 4, 1990

Inner Space and the Interior of the Maternal Body: Unfolding in the Psychoanalytical Process

Juan Francisco Jordan

This paper is a psychoanalytic investigation into the experience of space in a schizoid borderline patient. Its aim is to show the correlation between mental space, corporeal space and the fantasy of the interior of the mother's body. This correlation can be viewed, in the light of Matte-Blanco's reconceptualization of the unconscious, as a symmetrical experience of being as a fused relation with the mother's body. The unfolding of this fantasy is followed in the psychoanalytic process of the patient. A hypothesis of the genesis of the difficulties in the development of asymmetrically discriminated spaces is offered. The psychoanalytic process allows the unfolding of symmetrical being in the transference. By way of this unfolding the patient's consciousness can start to discriminate his own space as different from the mother's body.

The Values of Psychotherapy by Jeremy Holmes and Richard Lindley. Published by Oxford University Press, 1989; 206 pages; £7.90 paperback, 1991.

Robert Tollemache

Robert Tollemache

Robert Tollemache  

Holmes and Lindley's book offers a double vision of the values of psychotherapy. It reflects the interests of both authors, a consultant psychotherapist and a philosopher; it looks at the value of psychotherapy in society as well as values within psychotherapy; and it is concerned with both psychoanalytic psychotherapy and with many other kinds of therapy.

The first part focuses on the value of psychotherapy in society. Their review of the findings suggests that there is increasing evidence that it is both effective and cost effective. They advance ethical arguments for making it more widely and uniformly available and publicly funded; and that other and less extensive treatments such as brief, behavioural, humanistic and community therapy should be introduced or more widely used where appropriate. They review and reject the Marxist and libertarian objections that psychotherapy is a mere palliative to the evils of society, arguing for its liberating and hence potentially subversive, nonconformist nature.

The second part concentrates on some ethical problems within the practice of psychotherapy. The principle of non-self-disclosure raises the problem of how truthful the therapist can be while saying nothing about himself; they explore the temptation for therapists to impose their own version of the truth; and they stress the necessity for both supervision and internal supervision to get over these and other dilemmas as they arise. They raise other ethical problems including the use of paradoxical interventions, how the patient can give informed consent to his treatment, and the possibility of sexual or financial exploitation within psychotherapy. They also consider the use of therapy in coercive contexts like prison, and the problem of maintaining confidentiality when it might put the life or limb of others at risk.

The third part brings the social and the internal worlds of psychotherapy together in looking at the future development of the profession of psychotherapy; they prefer the idea of a code of practice to a code of ethics, they trace the way that the regulation and control of psychotherapy has developed so far, and press for it to become a distinct profession with its own institutions independent of the ‘core’ professions, controlling practice and entry to the profession.

The Brazilian Lectures by W R Bion. Published by Karnac Books; 1990; 213 pages; £16. 95 paperback.

David Mann

David Mann

David Mann  

The re-publication of this book gives those of us who missed it first time around a welcome chance to add it to our libraries. Unlike the extremely difficult four volumes which constitute The Seven Servants, these lectures present Bion at his most articulate, that is to say, minus large numbers of references to The Grid and to his algebraic abbreviations. Coltart (1990) remarks that Bion is uniquely forthcoming in these lectures. We can only speculate that the fact of having to talk through an interpreter encouraged him to explain himself more than was his usual custom.

There is no given subject or topic to the lectures. ‘Lectures’ also seems to imply the presenter reading a pre-written paper. This is not the case here. ‘Seminar’ comes closer as a description but even this has its limitations. The only two things which bind these ‘Lectures’ are the. place, two cities in Brazil, and the time, that they occurred between 1973-74. The reason why I have questioned the term ‘lectures’ is that ‘free associations’ might be a better description. Bion freely associates to a certain audience in Brazil in 1973-73. The audience, interestingly, respond in kind. (Even the ugly painting on the book cover, called Improvisation, mirrors this theme of free association.)

The tone of this approach to the lecture is set right at the beginning with Bion's evocative use of the grave robbers of the Royal Cemetery at Ur as a metaphor for therapy, whereby both client and therapist need to experience fear in response to the unknown which faces them. Like all metaphors this breaks down if examined too closely; therapy after all is not about theft of the self, but this metaphor serves to set the mood of the lectures, namely that Bion and his audience are embarking on unknown territory.

How much Bion and his audience are communicating at an unconscious level is quite striking. In one lecture, number 6 in Rio de Janeiro (pp. 123-132), a member of the audience gives a clinical example of a client who killed a pedestrian in a road accident. In the following lecture, Bion gives a clinical example of a client killed in a road accident. As neither Bion nor the audience link the two examples it is difficult to escape the conclusion that the questioner had affected Bion's unconscious, leading him to free associate on the same subject the following day, which in turn is suggestive of how much Bion was able to use his unconscious in a creative way.

Dear Sir

Your readers might like to know that the European Association for Transcultural Group Analysis was set up in 1986 by a group of European psychoanalysts and group analysts who had been working together for some four years. It aims to promote research into the cultural foundations of groups and of personality, an area which has been relatively neglected, but is of pressing importance with the increase in social disruption through migration, and intercultural conflict.

Since its founding, the Association has organised intercultural workshops in Maastricht (Holland), Heidelberg (Germany) and in Oxford, in which many people have participated who work in the fields of mental health, education and training, organisational consultation, social and cultural work.

A first international Symposium will be held at the University of Bologna (Italy) from 16th to 18th April 1992. Experiences on the following themes will be presented and discussed: (1) effects on individuals and groups of changes in political and social systems, migration and intercultural conflict. (2) identity, identification and the cultural foundations of personality. (3) clinical and psychotherapeutic experiences in groups concerning these topics. (4) research in the inter- and trans-cultural fields.

There will be a main lecture each morning, with a text available in Italian, German, French and English, and separate discussion groups in each language. In the afternoon there will be shorter papers and discussion in any of these languages, and poster sessions. Offers of papers are invited to be sent to: Dr Jaak Le Roy, Koning Albertlaan 154, B-3360 Bierbeek, Belgium.

I will be happy to provide further information. (Address: 88 Montagu Mansions, London W1H 1LF.

Editorial

R Hinshelwood

R Hinshelwood

R Hinshelwood  

There is not much in favour of hating the patient. And yet we must all do it; just as, according to Winnicott's plausible aphorism, all mothers hate their babies. Alan Prodgers draws attention to this and the importance of being aware of such countertransference disasters; and indeed of the ways in which it affects the therapeutic relationship. Without that counter-transference awareness the psychotherapist is at risk (and so is the patient) from the psychotherapist's defensiveness, from his method for dealing with the consequent guilt and, as Prodgers emphasises, the role that hate has in the motivation for treating the patient. Such an obstacle course for the psychotherapist's mind may never allow him to reach the potential usefulness of these counter-transference communications; though the art of psychotherapy is to keep on with that struggle.

But the negative aspects of the relationships our patients sustain with us is not the only tribulation we have to endure. There is, as often pointed out in this Journal, the intense negative relations amongst psychotherapists themselves. We are a cliquey lot. Peggy Jones describes a journey through her own encounter with certain psychotherapeutic writings which she characterises as the American self-help movement. Selfhelp and self-actualisation have a peculiarly American ring to them in the European ear; and a characteristically divided response. Jones has clearly tried to suffer that ambivalence and to come out with a balanced judgement on what she found. It is an exemplary process that perhaps we pursue each day with our patients; and then give up on as we relax from the daily grind and contemplate our colleagues from other schools of psychotherapy. Where, it is worth asking, does our own hostility go? To the UKSCP?

If the assessment of hate is an important counter-transference indicator in the pinpointing of the more disturbed forms of psychopathology, I have in my own paper in this issue tried to show the place that working through in the counter-transference has within the broad context of assessing the patient. In particular the centrality of the psychodynamic formulation is stressed in assessing the suitability for psychotherapy.
