Eric Rhode

Eric Rhode

Eric Rhode  

Martha Harris, to whom this book is fittingly dedicated, was among the first to see how the topography of the depressive position, as mapped out by Melanie Klein and some of her followers, had unexpectedly re-discovered, and from a quite breath-taking angle, the life in imagination that Coleridge and Keats in particular had described almost two hundred years before. Psychoanalysis, the authors inform the reader, is ‘the true child of literature’.

Placing the imaginative at the core of human understanding has widespread implications. It reforms social anthropology, theology and philosophy, as well as psychoanalysis, into a single discipline, concerning itself with mind as poetic.

The original model for this understanding is to be found in the living out of the oceanic, often dangerous and awesome Shakespearean experience. It is in Shakespeare, with whom the authors begin and in whom they find their framework, that a realisation of the imagination, brought from wild Platonic shores, ramifies into the uses of language as a modality of dreaming, in which the words of inspiration are indistinguishable from the elements of dream; it is at this moment that the English find their identity as pirates and unruly colonialists transformed into another equally hazardous manner of voyaging by way of ‘strange seas of thought’ as Wordsworth memorably called it at the end of his life.

Shakespeare is more a culture or climate than a hero of the imagination; conceivably, he is like the dream function itself. The authors discover their actual highrisk heroes in Milton and the Romantic poets, some of whom foundered terribly.

In a letter of 1818, Keats wrote:

The difference of high Sensations with and without knowledge appears to be this - in the latter case we are falling continually ten thousand fathoms deep and being blown up again without wings and with all [the] horror of a bare shouldered Creature - in the former case, our shoulders are fledge, and we go thro' the same air and space without fear.

Some Thoughts on Sibling Rivalry and Competitiveness

Gertrud Mander

Gertrud Mander

24 Chalcot Crescent, London NW1 8YD.

Gertrud Mander  

This paper was presented to the Fifth Conference of the Institute of Psychotherapy and Counselling whose overall subject was Envy. I chose the subject of sibling rivalry because I have always found it a burning personal issue. Surprisingly not much has been written about it; so I hoped it would be interesting for a change to think about an aspect of envy that is a universal experience and yet different from the primary envy which Melanie Klein located in the motherbaby relationship and the state of part object relating. Rivalry and competition begin in the later developmental phase when the infant has achieved unit status, and when the two-person relationship has expanded into three- and multi-person relationships where the issues are loss, exclusion and intrusion. Then the experience of difference and otherness has to be mastered so that socialisation can take place.

Eleanor Perlman

Eleanor Perlman

Eleanor Perlman  

Dr Sutherland was first Fairbairn's pupil, then his analysand, and later his colleague and friend. His obvious respect and affection for his subject are apparent.

Sutherland elaborates the connection between Fairbairn's troubled inner life and his theory. He centres his account on Fairbairn's relationships with his parents. But he also sets Fairbairn's life in its cultural context; Scotland with its tensions as the legacy of enlightened thinking of individuals such as Hume constrained by the moralistic climate of Calvinism with its glorification of work and suspicion of joy and sexuality. These values influenced Fairbairn's parents and through them Fairbairn himself.

Sutherland's respect for his colleague does not lead to idealisation. He gives a portrayal of a troubled man trying to make sense of his own neurosis. He makes use of Fairbairn's private self-analytic notes to illustrate this struggle. Sutherland also emphasises the institutional factors that influenced Fairbairn's professional development and possible professional advancement. This emphasises Fairbairn's thesis that the need for acceptance and relatedness does not only constrain the development of a separate differentiated self in the first three years of life. It is an ongoing hazard.

Fairbairn was trying to comprehend and integrate his clinical experience in relative isolation in the then psychoanalytic desert of Edinburgh. A desert that Dr Sutherland and other colleagues have done much to alter with the establishment of the Scottish Institute of Human Relations.

Nameless Revenge

A Brafman

A Brafman

A Brafman  

I had an interesting experience during a recent diagnostic interview. I found it unusual enough to recount to several colleagues and this provided me with a further interesting experience in that my story provoked very diverse reactions and interpretations from the listeners. So, here is a written account where I shall try to describe the events as they unfolded. Clearly, this is not the full interview but only the details that I consider relevant to convey both the patient's story and my own involvement.

Miss Brown is in her early forties. An attractive and intelligent woman, she is a highly competent professional who had considerable insight into her feelings and those of others. She decided to have psychotherapy because she felt she had never managed to bring her pursuits to a full, proper conclusion. From a working-class background, Miss Brown had made her way to university where she achieved considerable success and was encouraged to join the teaching staff. After a time she realised she was not happy and moved on to another activity: again, her repeated promotions were accompanied by a feeling of unhappiness and an incapacity to get her writings ready for publication. A new career was started and further successes followed and Miss Brown came to see me at the point where the culmination of her efforts appeared, again, to be thwarted.

In her personal life the pattern was not much different. She was able to form long and meaningful relationships but the men she chose ‘only seem to want to use me’. She had always wanted to have a child but here she was at an age where further pain appeared, in view of the realisation that she might have left it too late.

Right at the beginning of the interview, Miss Brown voiced her intense resentment against her mother. Now in her late seventies and severely demented this mother was blamed for having always tried to subject Miss Brown into total conformity. An older son from a previous marriage was ‘written oft’ because she did not approve of the woman he chose, relations were invariably described with contempt and hatred, the husband was tormented and abused - and Miss Brown could give endless examples of her mother's behaviour. She added that a charitable explanation would emphasise her mother's bitterness and sense of isolation, resulting from a lifetime of seeing herself as a victim, but Miss Brown found it quite difficult to make excuses for her mother. No doubt, she sensed that her mother's approaching death might signify another crisis in her life and she wanted to obtain help before that occurred.

Creative Envy or ‘Shiva Dancing Our Destruction’

Nigel Groom

Nigel Groom

Nigel Groom  

This paper is essentially about Envy as creative, as being about construction and destruction, about bringing Eros, Pan and Shiva into the relationship between therapist and client. It is an attempt to speak about sexualising, bodying, playing and the embodying of Envy as aggressive fantasy and activity out of the Imaginal world as I experience it with my clients.

‘Or Shiva Dancing our Destruction’ (Tippett 1983, p. 9) refers to Shiva as Cosmic Dancer, mystical yet ever-present, containing construction and destruction, chaos and order, inseparable opposites which manifest and arise out of the Imaginal world, the Mundus Imaginalis (Corbin 1972). I want to show what kind of underlying aggressive fantasies and activities around envy of the parents'/client's/therapist's or analyst's bodies become manifest in the work and how the primal metaphor of Shiva's dance underlies this in a powerful way.

Lionel Monteith

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles  

Lionel Monteith, the founder of the Lincoln Clinic & Institute for Psychotherapy, died suddenly on January 15th 1991. Lionel was born in 1921, and lived in Southborough and Brighton. His childhood was unhappy and the scars of these early years left Lionel prone to quite severe bouts of depression. It was only through psychoanalysis and his marriage that these wounds could begin to heal.

He left school at 15 and trained as a Quantity Surveyor. In 1953 he married Mary Huson, who was at the time a clinical tutor and antenatal sister at the London Hospital Annexe, and so began a long and creative marriage in which Mary played an essential part in encouraging Lionel's true gifts as both a psychotherapist and an administrator to emerge. Lionel had by this time found psychological help from Dr Percy Backus - he was later to have a long analysis with Dr Ladislaw Haas who had been an analysand of Otto Fenichel - and he was beginning to realise how essential therapy had been to him. He saw how limited this type of help still was for the majority of people, and he determined to try and do something about this. He thought that he might be able to help people best through the ministry. He enrolled at New College, London, and because of Mary's financial support, he was able to study for the next four years. He obtained a diploma in theology and in 1957, four days after his twin son and daughter had been born, he was ordained, and became the Congregational Minister at West Kensington. For the next seven years he tried to find a way in which he could incorporate his psycho-analytic experience into his pastoral duties. The Reverend Dr Leslie Weatherhead and the Reverend Dr Harry Guntrip were among his friends at this time, and they also were trying to create similar links. It became increasingly difficult to find the time to combine both jobs, Lionel was by this time working part-time as an affiliated psychotherapist at University College Hospital, but also he discovered that the Church was not supportive of his endeavour. This was the experience that Harry Guntrip was having and he wrote to Lionel saying that the Church did ‘not want to be awakened and will resist it with all their ability to rationalise their unrealised anxieties.’ (1)

This paper addresses why 9000 psychosomatic inpatient treatment places exist in Germany and how they are used. First, two case histories are presented to illustrate the particular patients and the typical problems that are dealt with by these units as well as the kind of approach used. This is followed by an outline of the preconditions for this, and a sketch of the actual state of psychosomatic inpatient treatment, illustrated by referring to the treatment approach in Heidelberg. Finally, outcome studies will be discussed.

Wounded Healer

Edward Moss

Edward Moss

Edward Moss  

I found Nathan Field's Post-Platonic Dialogue about Dr W- in your Winter issue (Vol. 7(2), pp. 141-147) both penetrating and moving. Dr W-, who in the practice of his profession ‘was a lover in the truest sense’, appeared differently to each of his patients. His guiding spirit was finally identified as that of the wounded healer, Chiron. This made me wonder whether a deeper identification might not be with a different wounded healer, of whom Eliot wrote, in reference to dying and the redemption of the Cross:

The wounded surgeon plies the steel

That questions the distempered part;

The sharp compassion of the healer's art

Resolving the enigma of the fever chart.

Another wounded healer with his own ‘thorn in the flesh’ who shared this identification was Paul; and significantly Paul once said that he was made all things to all men. As Kipling put it in the poem At His Execution:

I have forgot or foregone

The self men call their own

(Being made all things to all men) So that I might save some …

Kipling ends his poem with the line ‘Restore me my self again!’ But this does not quite strike the right note for Paul, the psychologist of the old false self and the new true self, conformed to Christ and so set free. It was the new self that he wanted. He made explicit his own guiding spirit: ‘not I, but Christ in me’.

Further Learning from the Patient; The Analytic Space and Process by Patrick Casement. Published by Tavistock/Routledge, 1990; £9.99 paperback.

Diana Bremner

Diana Bremner

Diana Bremner  

As in his earlier book Learning from the Patient published in 1985, Casement invites us to identify with him and with his patient as they work together analytically, and to reflect on the separate and connected experience of each. He shows how, by practising ‘trial identification’ with the patient and his inner world, he is enabled as therapist to respond in ways which provide space and time for the patient's emotional experience to develop meaning and connect with the rest of his life.

Casement is already well known to a wide public in the helping professions for his gift in conveying complex human interaction in simple English, illustrated with precisely selected and focused clinical material, and his new book is in the same style. He also discusses the approach to the psychotic, what is therapeutic in psychoanalysis and psychotherapy, and training: implicitly, as well as explicitly, he provokes thinking about these issues.

In Chapter 3, ‘A child leads the way’, the meaning of analytic space and process is beautifully illuminated by an account of a child therapy. Both patient and therapist have their anxieties, the child pushing for growth and afraid of discovering what she needs to know; while Casement, as a young and as yet unqualified therapist, is afraid of trespassing professionally; he had been engaged as a remedial tutor. Yet the evidence is there that he was unconsciously feeling and responding, even as he delayed, to the child's fears and growing readiness to use the freedom of the analytic space which she prompted him to negotiate with her mother. This therapy is an achievement: that its effectiveness was long-lasting is confirmed by the Follow-Up. The Discussion, therefore, at the end of the chapter has a discordant note of apology and challenge, as if addressed to some ‘classical’ judge dispensing qualifications from the heights of Olympus or Sinai, and blind to the internal qualifications manifested in the young Casement.

The background presence of a dogmatic analyst (or group of analysts) revisited me from time to time as I read the book. Casement's profound concern is that patients may be protected from the rigid theoretical (pseudo-analytical) approach which blocks space and process: but in his efforts to further understanding he himself sometimes seems to become the arbitrary teacher who ‘knows’, imposing his view and providing the reader with the same emotional experience from which he wishes to preserve the patient. It is worth reflecting on this dialectic which occurs in many learning situations.

[[RunningHead]]

Parents as Messengers

Andrew Samuels

Andrew Samuels

17 Archibald Road, London N7 0AN.

Andrew Samuels  

Some unexpected implications and meanings of parental material and imagery are advanced. It is suggested that, broadly speaking, the parents function as messengers. Three hypotheses are offered: (1) what is described to the therapist as a negative parental attribute can also be understood as representing something positive that the individual needs to develop in him or herself, or as a kind of unconscious agenda suggesting emotional difficulties that need to be worked on in therapy; (2) parental imagery tells the therapist something about the patient's level of political development, expressed in the form of their parenting capacity. This capacity is conceived as the individual's whole attitude to other people, and to the external world in general - his or her position on political and cultural issues included; (3) primal scene imagery functions as a kind of psychic fingerprint or trademark, indicating the state of play or overall situation in the patient's psyche. The primal scene, like other forms of parental imagery, is a self-generated diagnostic, holistic monitoring of the patient's psychological state. Once again, parental imagery such as that of the primal scene indicates the patient's capacity to tolerate political conflict in the external social situation as well as conflict in the inner world. Illustrations of these hypotheses are given. The paper goes on to discuss: (1) how literal statements concerning the parents can bear metaphorical meanings at the same time; (2) why the parents in particular do the job of messenger; (3) the impact of these ideas on interpretation, leading to remarks about plural interpretation; (4) Jung's concept of the objective psyche; (5) the metaphor of messenger. Finally, some parellels between analytical psychology and psychoanalysis are drawn.

Mothering Psychoanalysis sets out to tell the story of a ‘revolution’ in psychoanalysis from a ‘father-centered phallocentrism’ to a ‘mother-centered’ focus. The author attempts to do so through a series of self-contained biographies of four leading women psychoanalysts influential in Freud's day - Helene Deutsch, Karen Homey, Anna Freud and Melanie Klein. In addition to presenting their life stories Janet Sayers gives a lucid and mostly faithful rendering of their work. As such, this is a useful book for the student or layperson with an interest in psychoanalytic ideas. Nevertheless, one would hope this book whets their appetite to read the papers in their original form as much is inevitably lost in condensing them.

Despite my pleasure in having the work of these four women introduced to a new readership, I must point out some shortcomings, as I see them, in the hope that they may be rectified in subsequent editions. It seems to me that Janet Sayers clips her own intellectual wings by not drawing conclusions.

The Goals of Psychoanalysis: Identification, Identity and Supervision by Leon Grinberg. Published by Karnac Books, London, 1991; 404 pages; £18.00 paperback.

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon  

This volume brings together more than two dozen papers by the Spanish psychoanalyst, Leon Grinberg, a former vice-president of the International Psychoanalytic Association and currently Professor of Psychoanalysis at the Ateneo de Madrid. Many of these papers have never been published before in English.

Almost half the book is concerned with two concepts which lie at the heart of the psychoanalytic undertaking, yet which are rarely scrutinised - the notions of identification and identity. The former is for Grinberg ‘central and basic to the understanding of the development and organisation of the personality’, a fundamental process in the formation of the ego, super-ego and ego ideal, character and identity since ‘it is a constant in the interplay between subject and objects’.

Starting with a lucid exposition of the theory of identification as expounded by Freud and by those who came after him, Grinberg goes on to examine the relationship between identification and internalisation on the one hand and externalisation on the other. The former includes processes such as incorporation, assimilation, imitation and introjection; the latter, extrojection, projection and, of course, projective identification. This latter is given especial examination, and the development of the concept from Klein through Bion, Rosenfeld and Meltzer charted. In doing so, Grinberg presents a careful elucidation of a concept, greatly used, perhaps overly so and much misunderstood, in which different aims and modes are distinguished.

Grinberg also puts forward a theory of what he calls projective counteridentification. By this he means a specific reaction which arises in the analyst as the result of the excessive intervention of projective identification by the analysand. In such cases, the analyst ‘ceases to be himself and turns unavoidably into what the patient unconsciously wants him to be’. This may sound similar to Racker's concept of ‘complementary countertransference’. The difference, however, is that projective counteridentification is largely independent of the analyst's own conflicts and corresponds predominantly or exclusively with the intensity and quality of the patient's projective identification. Just as counter-transference can be an aid rather than hindrance in clinical work so, Grinberg argues, projective counteridentification maybe necessary to reach a state of ‘convergence’ with the anxiety, pain or delirium of the patient. Indeed, it is an essential part of what Grinberg regards as the analyst's function, that is ‘the ability to regress, to let himself be invaded, and to “place himself within the patient's productions, even psychotic, experiencing together with him the emotions contained within them, and being able to return to external reality’.

[[RunningHead]]

Listening to Silence

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini  

I have examined the function of silence - its possible role and meanings - in the psychoanalytic encounter. I have argued that silence is complementary to words in general, and to analytic free-associations in particular, and that silence in the patient is often more than just the expression of his resistance.

It could be useful to consider the silent space within a session as a sort of container of words - words that, for complex, overdetermined, unconscious reasons cannot be uttered. I have insisted on the significance of analytic silences and warned against responding to them either through a retaliatory silence or through a flood of premature interpretations. These inadequate reactions often stem from the analyst's own anxiety evoked in him by the patient's silence.

Anxiety and silence are closely connected. Each silence is a compromise formation, concealing the unconscious fantasy from which it originates, while expressing a conscious one, often related to the transference situation. It is the task of the analyst to listen to his patient's silences in order to help him understand their meanings.

Skin That Has No Roots

Robin Balbernie

Robin Balbernie

Gloucester GL1 3PX

Robin Balbernie  

Introduction

The ego is a heuristic term, rather than an entity, which we employ to indicate the location of our sense of who we are. This sense has two main aspects: tactile and verbal, or sensation and sensibility. In the unconscious these ambiguities interact and may be inseparable. There is a dynamic process whereby we learn to feel ourselves; the ego is owned within the confines of the body, taking the similarity of limits for granted, while, in health, maintaining sufficient flexibility for psychological exchange between outer and inner.

The surface of the body is of tremendous importance. It is the site of physical sensations which once defined a psychological event, the beginning of the ego, and it continues to be the bodily counterpart of the sense of identity. Skin can be both a signal and a source of emotions (and I would include here a negative spectrum from blushing to self-mutilation with a positive one from hugging to sexuality) central to the sort of person we feel ourselves to be. In one way, what we might call the sensation-ego is a boundary to the verbal-ego as well as each being a component of the other while, in another way, it can provide a site for manifestly abnormal actions or ideas.

There follows an account of the treatment of an adolescent girl with a long history of gross obsessional-compulsive symptoms which had culminated in a set of phobic behaviours centred on AIDS. These were making normal life impossible. As in all psychotherapy, words were used to alter what was felt. We can be touched by what is spoken. In this case it was her sense of skin that made sense and led to change.

Presenting Problem

Jane was referred with a dramatic range of obsessional-compulsive thoughts and behaviours which circled around her dual fascination with AIDS. She was certain that she either had it and was a danger to others, or that she was permanently at risk of contracting it. She thought of little else and behaved accordingly.

She was also aware that her outlook was not confirmed by logic; but this sense of being almost compelled against her will had simply increased her anxieties and had virtually trapped her in what seemed like an obsessional neurosis where, as described by Freud (1916), she was occupied by thoughts in which she was not in fact interested; she was aware of impulses in herself which appeared very strange to her and was led to actions the performance of which gave her no enjoyment. She was obliged against her will to brood and speculate as though it were a question of her most vital problems (my paraphrase).

Bernard Ratigan

Bernard Ratigan  

The incidence of HIV and AIDS is increasing in Britain. Many of those affected are subjected to, and subject others to, powerful psychological pressures. Hitherto, the psychological care of such patients has been much influenced by cognitive-behavioural approaches and only more recently have psychodynamic insights been brought into focus. This paper reports psychotherapeutic work undertaken both directly with HIV and AIDS patients, their partners and families and with clinical teams providing medical care.

The paper attempts to begin to sketch out a map of the psychodynamics of HIV and AIDS to encourage a better understanding of how clinicians can be helped to understand how psychosocial attitudes can be passed on to patients in the form of unconscious attacks and how patients can cause severe acting out on the part of clinicians as they try to resolve their own unconscious conflicts over their illness.

Christopher Clulow  

It is hard to imagine a worse situation for a couple to face than the terminal illness of their child. High material standards and advanced medical technology have exposed few parents to first-hand experience of losing a child. For some, however, they have converted the acute trauma of certain death into the long-term stresses associated with chronic illness and its uncertain course. This paper describes the nature of some of the stresses on family members, paying particular attention to the parental couple. Through detailed consideration of one couple's experience, the internal ramifications for marriage of a child who is seriously and chronically ill are examined, and consideration is given to the effectiveness in these circumstances of anticipatory mourning and other forms of help.

Shame and the Problem of Suicide: A Family Systems Perspective

Melvin Lansky

Melvin Lansky

1100 Glendon Avenue, Suite 1527, Los Angeles, CA 90024.

Melvin Lansky  

Shame, a major yet neglected regulatory affect, is the emotion signalling threat to significant social bonding. Shame is often hidden or veiled by depression, guilt, anger or nonspecific psychic pain. Suicidal persons become flooded with shame if optimal distance to supportive persons is not maintained and the patient feels overregulated, abandoned or exposed as incapable of sustaining meaningful attachments. Details of the patient's sense of shame and protective manoeuvres to avoid shame should be sought in the patient's early familial background. Shame dynamics in current familial functioning or dysfunction should be clarified for effective clinical intervention. Illustrative cases are presented.

Feminism and Psychoanalytic Theory by Nancy Chodorow. Published by Polity Press, Cambridge; 1990; £25 hardback.

Janet Sayers

Janet Sayers

Janet Sayers  

Object relations theory, with its insistence on the social matrix of infant individuation, seems peculiarly well-suited to the feminist project of marrying social and psychoanalytic theory. Certainly this is the view developed in this collection of essays by US sociologist Nancy Chodorow.

She first airs themes familiar from her influential book The Reproduction of Mothering. Assuming teleologically, with functionalist sociology, that gender identity is a goal of development, Chodorow argues that in boys this identity is formed through negation of their earliest female-based identification with the mother - this in implicit contrast to the centrality accorded by Freud to phallic difference and the father in the genesis of sexed identity. Chodorow's contrary mothering thesis is instead elaborated in terms of Fairbairn's and Mahler's account of the infant's initial psychological oneness with the mother and subsequent separation-individuation from her. Individuation in boys, claims Chodorow, is precipitated by the mother's experience of their sexual difference from her. By contrast, and here Chodorow cites clinical evidence, mothers tend to over-identify with their daughters. The latter accordingly turn to the father not to gain a penis, as Freud claimed, but to separate from the mother. Men are therefore secondary to the mother in women's psychology, the resulting ‘heterosexual knots’ being the subject of Chodorow's next paper. Lastly, she ascribes to women's mothering our society's prevalent idealisation and excoriation of mothers and its emphasis on gender difference - the latter being an effect, she maintains, of men's need to stress such difference in establishing a separate male identity.

Going beyond these Reproduction of Mothering themes, the second half of this book is devoted to arguing the general superiority of object relations over instinct theory. First Chodorow deplores Herbert Marcuse and Norman Brown's celebration of individual instinct against its social repression in answering Freud's account of the conflict of individual and society. They thereby falsely imply, argues Chodorow, that individuality is essentially constrained by social relations when in fact the latter - the infant's initial psychological fusion with the mother - is the very precondition of its individuality coming into being. Furthermore, and in the tradition of those opposed to the social philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, Chodorow rejects both sociologists' ‘radical individualism’ in urging return to self-serving primary narcissism and polymorphous perversity to the neglect of the child's development toward recognition of others, not as mere servants of the self, but as also having their own independent subjectivity. Chodorow continues this theme in contrasting Freud's instinct and object relations theories.

[Because the session presented here derives from an orientation (systems theory) different from that of analytical psychotherapy, the therapists concerned have in this instance preferred not to remain anonymous and to preface the session with a brief introduction of their way of working.

The material has been sent to three people who represent different psychotherapeutic schools of thought. They have been asked to comment on the material and the approach of the therapist in the session. The intention is to put these commentaries on the same material side by side for comparison of the different approaches and to facilitate the understanding of alternative terminologies and modes of practice - Ed]

Introduction

Presenting this brief case study to the Journal poses us with a dilemma. It is quite possible that most of the readership will not share our theoretical orientation. So, in this context, how can we present an aspect of our work that is both useful and interesting yet not need the reader to be familiar with, nor require a full explanation of, our working model? We have decided to present an episode which we hope will highlight the practice aspect of our work. The episode we focus on is from the final stage of therapy and is intended to give some indication of movement in the therapeutic process.

We have summarised the earlier stages of therapy but have not the space here to elaborate on issues that were considered in depth during the therapy. In spite of this brevity we hope that readers will find this paper interesting, informative and of some potential use in their own practice.

The example we have chosen is a therapeutic ritual which is enacted within a family therapy session. We think this case has the potential to be interesting and useful in a variety of ways to therapists of different persuasions.

Our practice is within a model of therapy that has come to be known as a ‘systemic approach’. This approach has developed out of our work in family therapy, in particular the Milan Model, though other systemic practitioners have arrived at a similar position from different pathways. For those readers who wish to explore the systemic approach in more detail we have included a selected reading list at the end of the article.

Commentary by a Pragmatic/Eclectic Family Therapist Team Using a Systemic Approach

Roger Benady and Margaret Fox

Margaret Fox

Margaret Fox  

We are offered a little gem: an illustration of a piece of work with a satisfying

101

emotional ‘outcome’. The approach used took into account family life cycles, transitional events, ‘rites of passage’ and task setting. The rifts between the parents have healed and they can move their separate ways; the daughter's development is not compromised and even the therapist needs a hanky to wipe away a tear. Rich stuff!

Any criticism therefore seems to be carping unduly at minutiae. The therapy seems to have worked, so praise it, look at the process, admire the skill, the alliances the therapist made with all the members, the sensitivity of handling painful issues, the freedom of using individual therapy skills within a family context, and not least the visualisation of change to enable the family the freedom to move on. So what is the nagging doubt?

We are told (and are not told) some of the context and initial problems. Who did refer this family? Was Jane's weight ever considered sufficiently low to warrant actually knowing it? The family have separated for seven years, i.e. since Jane was six years old, and one can only infer that she was living with her mother. Hints are also given about Jane's difficulty at identification with her mother and her own sexuality. How did the therapist obtain the background information? There certainly seems to have been a mother/daughter conflict and possible power struggle. We do not know if that was addressed or deliberately not addressed. One wonders what had to happen to destabilise the system; that is, Jane becoming symptomatic. Was it probably father returning to his own country - or was it mother entering yet another relationship at the expense of closenss to Jane?

We could not help wondering after reading Furman and Aloha's article (1989) whether the intervention had been intuitively arrived at and the process worked out backwards to meet the intervention.

At the most basic level we have no quarrel with the therapists. They did open up communication, and enabled the family to open out their perceptions of each other. Undoubtedly however, we would have had our myths about the development of eating disorders in adolescents. Would we, I wonder, have been tempted to look at issues of power and anger in the system as well as issues of grief and separation? Would the feminists in our team have addressed the changing relationship of mother, not just to her ex-husband and daughter, but also to her ‘new lesbian relationship’? Would they have been concerned over Jane's developing sexuality as well as her feelings of insecurity to the forthcoming change with her father returning to his country? What would have been the effect of looking at Jane's triangulation between her mother and father and between her mother and her new partner? This would have been a rich seam to explore in the process of famil work.

Response to John Rowan

Robert Whyte

Robert Whyte

Robert Whyte  

Thank you for your letter and for your interest in my paper, ‘Giving and Taking: The Foetal-Maternal Placental Junction as a Prototype and Precursor of Object Relations’.

You take issue with a number of points in the theoretical part. Firstly, I should like to admit freely to using, at times, a dogmatic style in what is speculative writing. Your letter, it seems to me, at times demonstrates a similar style.

Regarding the quotation from Laing, I have assumed that Freud's ‘version of the objective scientific scheme of things’ is the only version, and this is obviously not the case.

You say that Stern is not a researcher. In the bibliography of his book, there are twelve papers of which he is either the sole or joint author, which strongly suggests that he is a researcher. The perceptual memories of sounds heard in the womb, although quoted by Stern, were indeed not his own research but that of Lipsitt, personally communicated to Stern in 1984.

You say that none of the medical textbooks known to you mention a distinction between a foetal placenta and a maternal placenta, and also say that I do not quote evidence and so you are sceptical. However, I have given the reference to my source, i.e. Baird, D. (1962) Combined Textbook of Obstetrics and Gynaecology (E S Livingstone Ltd). On p. 74, it reads: ‘It is of great importance to remember that, although colloquially the afterbirth is called the placenta, yet this in reality only represents the foetal part. Biologically, the placenta is an organ developed by mother and child in symbiosis and can be defined anatomically as the chorion frondosum, the decidua basalis and the chorio-decidual space or blood lake between’.

Since receiving your letter, I have obtained and read your chapter ‘Primal Integration’ in Innovative Therapy in Britain. I was not previously aware of your work. I see that it covers some areas on which I have commented although your view of antenatal events is very different from mine. I could not comment just now on these differences without further study of your work. I am grateful to you for drawing attention to a number of works which had not previously come to my notice.

Warren Colman

Warren Colman

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA.

Warren Colman  

This paper provides a critical discussion of Klein's theory of envy as primary, an innate aspect of the destructive forces. The author argues that envy is the outcome of a defective mother/infant fit in which the infant's need for illusory omnipotence is not met, resulting in a sense of lack of sufficient internal resources to manage existence as a separate individual (i.e. feelings of worthlessness and helplessness). Envy arises from this sense of lack through the compensatory fantasy of an all-providing other who possesses the qualities required to fill the gap. If the gap is felt to be intolerable, destructive spoiling ensues as an attempt to obliterate it. This aspect of envy is therefore seen as ultimately defensive rather than, as in Klein's view, a primary impulse against which defences are instituted.

R Hinshelwood  

This paper describes one form of psychodynamic formulation. Three areas of object-relations (the current life situation, the early infantile relations and the transference relationship) are focused upon to derive a common pattern. From these core object-relationships a point of maximum pain can be hypothesised and the attendant defensive relationships. The paper also discusses the central importance of testing hypotheses with interpretation even in the assessment interview, and the prime interest of the psychodynamic formulation in assessing other factors in the suitability of a patient for psychotherapy.

Peter Bierenbroodspot

Peter Bierenbroodspot

Postbus 5, 2120 BA Bennebroek, Netherlands

Peter Bierenbroodspot  

In his daily work, guilt and shame and, consequently, punishment and penance do not pass over the psychoanalyst unobtrusively even if the ‘ideal’ basic psychoanalytic attitude demands that he/she be above this kind of human triviality. After all, through his own training analysis and through education he can be (or become) conscious of feelings contrary to the high psychoanalytic expectations of the person behind the couch: to listen patiently, not to react emotionally or aspire after direct gratification, be always understanding and unselfish, never offended, always aiming at insight and, in the end, to make himself redundant.

That is the ideal, but what is it like in reality? There is obviously a field of tension, caused not only by one's personal impediments, including one's personal motives to choose this profession, but also evoked by the conventions within one's professional group as a socially defined professional superego. How tolerant are psychoanalysts of each other, is this much aspired inner awareness, for example, actually facilitated or rather impeded, owing to the rigidity of the rules?

In any case, the personal superego and especially the ego ideal, in psychoanalysis partly transposed to a professional superego and a professional ideal image, play an important part and contribute to the ultimate result. Inner awareness still seems to be the main thing.

Fundamental Considerations in the Psychotherapy of an Identical Twin

Declan Sheerin

Declan Sheerin

Edinburgh EH 10 5HF

Declan Sheerin  

Identical twins encounter unique psychological and maturational difficulties alien to the experiences of single children. A brief review of the literature on these points is presented, emphasising both the tormenting and gratifying aspects of a twin who has in the outside world another identical self that the world notices and confuses with him. Such aspects need to be taken into consideration when engaging an identical twin in analytical psychotherapy. ‘Fallout’ from psychotherapy can have repercussions on those close to the patient but in the case of identical twins the effects on the twin not in therapy can be disastrous. In particular, when psychotherapy-by-proxy ensues it appears possible for the co-twin to establish strong links to the analyst through his narcissistic relationship with his twin, which appear transferential in nature. A clinical vignette is presented which elaborates on the issues of twin transference and the fallout effects on the twin not in therapy. A question is put forward: whether it is realistic to analyse identical twins individually and not together when their narcissistic dependency and defensive hostility are paramount to internal processes. The author takes the view that a psychoanalytical orientation to the psychotherapy of an identical twin is the most recommended but cautions against individual psychoanalytical psychotherapy where the real drive is the assassination of the internal and external twin-object as a means to individuation from the twinship. The nature of this object - whether selfobject or transformational object - is tentatively discussed.

Beauty and the Beast: The Father's Unconscious and the Riddle of Femininity

Christina Wieland

Christina Wieland

50 Femleigh Road, London N21 3AL

Christina Wieland  

This paper is about the importance of the father-daughter relationship in the development of femininity. It is the author's opinion that recent accounts of femininity have concentrated, in contrast to Freud, almost exclusively on the mother-daughter relationship thus ignoring the father and, most importantly, the father's unconscious masculinity and its influence on the development of femininity. The nature and development of masculinity and its relation to femininity are explored and the implications of these for the father-daughter relationship and for the development of the girl's sexual identity are examined. Phantasies, fears and anxieties about both masculinity and femininity, the collusion that develops between father and daughter, and the possible solutions and attempts at compromise that the girl develops are explored.

Hari Maharajh and Patricia Sarkar-Crooks

Patricia Sarkar-Crooks

Patricia Sarkar-Crooks  

The disclosure of a positive Human Immunodeficiency Viral (HIV) test to infected patients has prompted a cry for revenge directed towards themselves and society. AIDS revenge is a behavioural manifestation of a grief reaction variably influenced by the individual's perception of his illness and society's response to it. Many perceive an infection with the AIDS virus as a shameful death sentence, exposure of homosexual involvement and humiliation to the victim and his family. We wish to present three short cases. There appears to be a need for structured psychological treatment methods. The consultation-liaison psychiatrist or psychologist must be involved in treatment since they can identify serious problems before they present as medical emergencies.

Getting Established: Initiatives in Psychotherapy Training since World War Two

Jean Scarlett

Jean Scarlett

3 Byron Villas, Vale of Health, London NW3 IAR.

Jean Scarlett  

The decade before the first world war saw the gradual introduction of psychotherapy into this country. Suggestion techniques and the hypnosis pioneered by Charcot at the Salpetriere were imported from France. Jung's association tests were coming into use and the possibilities of dream interpretation and psycho-analysis were being explored. Ernest Jones founded the London Psycho-Analytical Society on 30 October 1913. The Tavistock, both as a clinic and training institution, had its beginnings in 1920 and the Brunswick Square Clinic flourished between 1913 and 1924. The years after the end of the second world war heralded an era of progess in new directions.

The story begins in 1950 when a group of gifted people came together, first in Oxford and then in Kensington, and took the first tentative steps, daring in those days, towards the formation of an association of psychotherapists. This was the core from which were to grow four bodies: the Association of Psychotherapists, now the British Association of Psychotherapists, the London Centre for Psychotherapy, the Association for Group and Individual Psychotherapy (AGIP) and the Guildford Centre and Society for Psychotherapy.

I did not arrive on this scene until the sixties so, for the early history, I am dependent on the accounts of the leading spirits of the enterprise, Paul and Patricia de Berker. They have both been persuaded to write the story in their own way and I have made an attempt to put the two versions together. These versions vary slightly in detail and sometimes in emphasis so I must ask the reader to forgive any little repetitions or inconsistencies which may occur.

Paul begins as follows: ‘In 1950 Patricia and I came down from Glasgow and set up our first house in Kensington. At that time, I was working as a psychologist in the Home Office Prison Department. I was very eager to see some therapeutic work set up there, especially amongst the Borstals, and also to establish a private practice in London.

‘In the 1950s the climate of opinion in the medical services and also the Civil Service was not conducive to psychotherapy. Very little was known about it and the two main training bodies, the Institute of Psycho-Analysis and the Society of Analytical Psychology, were seen as closely guarded, somewhat esoteric specialities who were very jealous of their particular knowledge and restrictive in their membership.

The Vale of Soul-Making: Psychotherapy and the Growth of the Mind

Margot Waddell

Margot Waddell

Belsize Lane, London NW3.

Margot Waddell  

Eschewing the conventional description of the world as a ‘vale of tears’, Keats protests that it be called rather ‘the vale of soul-making’ (1819, Letters, p. 249). He had earlier distinguished between those who are able genuinely to explore the further chambers, the inner recesses and dark passages, of what he had called the ‘large Mansion of Many Apartments’ - human life (the life of the mind), and those who stopped thinking or at least did not ‘think into the human heart’ (1818, Letters, pp. 95-96). The Soul-making, emphasis in the experience of life, lies in the capacity to tolerate the perception that ‘the World is full of Misery and Heartbreak, Pain, Sickness and oppression’ (Letters, p. 95), that knowledge being co-terminous with the realisation that it is in apprehending that very reality that the many doors open from the Chamber of Maiden Thought.

The human being's development - the progress from one chamber to another - from the first infant or thoughtless Chamber into the Chamber of Maiden Thought, with its ‘intoxicating light and pleasant wonders’, and beyond - that progress depends on the essentially mysterious process of what Keats describes as ‘the awakening of the thinking principle within us’. The system of Soul-making is Keats's description of the growth of the mind. For us children of the vale, the world of pains and troubles ‘schools’ our intelligence, if we allow it to. The learning takes place in a distinctive way. For the vale is the place where the heart must feel and suffer - the Heart is the Mind's Bible; the Mind's experience - ‘it is the teat from which the Mind or intelligence sucks its identity…’ (1819, Letters, p. 250). Here, in the vale, Man is formed by Circumstances, says Keats, ‘touchstones of his heart’, ‘proovings of his heart’, ‘fortifiers or alterers of his nature’. Identity is made, then, through the medium of the Heart in a world of Circumstances (Letters, p. 251). The process Keats describes is the essence of what Bion was later to call ‘learning from experience’.

Dream, Phantasy and Art by Hanna Segal. Published by Tavistock/Routledge, London, 1991; 120 pages; £10.99 paperback.

David Mann

David Mann

David Mann  

Hanna Segal's previous papers have established her as an outstanding contributor to the development of Kleinian theory in such areas as aesthetics, symbolism, dreams and psychotic thinking. This new book brings the reader up to date with her current thinking about these issues and much more.

It is worth saying at the outset that this book is very approachable and readable. This is not something that can be said about all Kleinian writers as Grotstein (1990) admits. In terms of writing style the book is clear, intelligible and the theoretical statements are richly illustrated with examples. It is easy to see why Segal has and deserves such a high reputation as a teacher.

The book is aimed at both the general reader as well as the psychoanalyst. With this in mind the first five chapters serve as an introduction to the basic ideas of Freud and the Kleinians. Chapter one, ‘The royal road’, begins with an outline of Freud's dream theory. The reader familiar with the basic concepts may well find the opening pages uninteresting and simplistic. I was a little disconcerted by the first couple of pages which suggested that the book might be aimed too much at the uninformed reader. My doubts, however, were quickly dispelled. The first two chapters focus on the theories of Freud and Klein. Not until the third chapter does Segal introduce some of her own original ideas. This chapter, on symbolism, restates her earlier conclusions about the role and function of symbolic equation and symbolic representation in the development of symbol formation and the maturation of the ego.

As Betty Joseph remarks in her Foreword to the book, the discussions become more complex from chapter four, ‘Mental space and elements of symbolism’, onwards. Segal integrates some of Bion's basic concepts - such as bizarre objects, container/contained apparatus and alpha/beta function processes - with her own idea of the third object, the father. The father's role has been rather back-stage in much of Kleinian theory, but here Segal proposes it is implicit in the depressive position in which the infant begins to recognise the mother as a whole person who has a life and relationships unrelated to the infant - primarily with the father. Father's role is seen partly as one which interrupts the mutual projective identifications between mother and baby and also in the creation of a new kind of mental space that is triangular: baby/mother, baby/father, mother/father. This triangular space becomes important for the development of thinking in the infant: ‘It is not “saturated” by mutual projections between mother and child. As a new, unsaturated, mental space it allows for the birth of new thoughts, two come together like parents in intercourse to produce a third new thought’ (p. 62). This strikes me as very plausible. My only reservation is that Segal does not make reference to how the mutual projective identifications between father and baby, or between father and mother as the birth of a new infant activates primitive phantasies in parents, find a place in this scheme.

Avoiding the Edge

Peggy Jones

Peggy Jones

52 The Vineyard, Richmond, Surrey TW10 6AT.

Peggy Jones  

The paper explores the question of whether and in what way psychotherapy may be a ‘dangerous’ profession. Starting with a recognition of personal hostility towards the American self-help approach, I consider why we as a profession may be unwilling to examine other approaches and explore the tension inherent in our work between our own ‘health’ and ‘woundedness’. I consider the dangers - personal and collective - of isolating and insulating ourselves against the wider social, cultural and political world and I assert that: ‘committing ourselves to finding and nurturing the source of responsibility, conscience, truth and freedom in others is not the same as committing ourselves to finding and nurturing that source in ourselves, or in the world’.
